Kneadingtroughs
nēd'ĭng-trôfs
n. pl. (the wooden bowls in which dough was worked; carried out of Egypt bound up in the people's clothes)
English knead, Old English cnedan, to work dough, with trough. The Hebrew mishereth is a kneading bowl; the same word appears in the plague of frogs, which came up into the very bowls the bread was made in.

Biblical Definition

The word marks the hour of the exodus: “And the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders” (Exo 12:34). The detail is domestic and enormous. There was no time to let the dough rise, so they wrapped the bowls in their outer garments and put them on their shoulders, and the unleavened bread of the Passover was the result rather than the plan: “And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual” (Exo 12:39). The instruction had already anticipated the haste: “And thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover” (Exo 12:11). The same bowls had been a battlefield in the plagues, when the frogs came up into the houses, into the bedchambers and into the kneadingtroughs of Egypt.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a kneading-trough as a trough or vessel in which dough is worked and mixed; and to knead as to work dough by pressing it with the hands.

expand to see more

KNEAD, v.t. To work and press dough or paste into a mass, usually with the hands.

KNEADING, ppr. Working and mixing into a well mixed mass, as dough.

KNEADING-TROUGH, n. A trough or vessel in which dough is worked and mixed.

Their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes. Ex. xii.

Key Scripture

Exo 12:34 — "And the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders."

Exo 12:39 — "And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual."

Exo 12:11 — "And thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover."

Exo 1:14 — "And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour."

Modern Corruption

The exodus is retold as a story of a people liberating themselves, when Exodus 12 has them thrust out with unrisen dough on their shoulders, having prepared no food at all.

expand to see more

Liberation readings of the exodus — whether in liberation theology or in the general political use the story receives every generation — make Israel the agent of her own deliverance and the exodus a template for movements. The text resists this at every point, and the kneadingtroughs are the small proof. Israel did not organise a departure; they were thrust out, could not tarry, and had prepared for themselves no victual. Everything decisive was done by God: the plagues, the death of the firstborn, the blood on the lintel, the hardening and then the breaking of Pharaoh. The people obeyed an instruction about a lamb, and ate standing up with their shoes on. Their whole contribution to the night was to be ready to leave and to be under the blood.

The unleavened bread is the second point and it becomes doctrine. They ate unleavened because there was no time, and God then commanded the feast of unleavened bread for ever, so that the accident of the night became a memorial and afterwards a figure. Paul draws it out: purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Egypt's bondage had been in morter and brick, and the same hands that had made bricks under rigour now carried bowls of unrisen dough out into the desert. Deliverance in Scripture is rarely tidy, and it is never self-generated.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mishereth (H4863), a kneading trough; with batseq (H1217), dough, and chippazon (H2649), haste — the word of the Passover's eating.

expand to see more

Hebrew mishereth (H4863) — a kneading trough; bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders; Exodus 12:34, Exodus 8:3.

Hebrew batseq (H1217) — dough; taken before it was leavened; Exodus 12:34.

Hebrew matstsah (H4682) — unleavened bread; the accident of a night made a perpetual feast; Exodus 12:39.

Hebrew chippazon (H2649) — haste, trepidation; ye shall eat it in haste; Exodus 12:11.

Greek zume (G2219) — leaven; purge out therefore the old leaven; 1 Corinthians 5:7.

Usage

"“Their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes” — the bowls went over the shoulder."

"“They were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry” — not a departure they arranged."

"“Ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover” — shoes on, staff in hand."
